text: Model extraction steals the model itself. These two attacks go after something quieter but arguably more sensitive — what the model's outputs reveal about the actual people whose records trained it. That makes this lesson a privacy lesson as much as a security one, and it sets up exactly why differential privacy, two lessons from now, is worth the math.

Model inversion uses a model's outputs — predictions, confidence scores, sometimes gradients — to reconstruct representative features of the inputs that produced them, without ever touching the training data directly. Fredrikson and colleagues' 2015 research reconstructed a recognizable face for a given name from a facial recognition API using only its own confidence-scored outputs, and separately recovered genetic markers from a model that was only supposed to output a drug dosage recommendation.

Membership inference asks a narrower question: given a specific record, was it part of this model's training set? Shokri and colleagues' 2017 paper formalized the mechanism behind it — overfitting. A model that has memorized its training data even slightly tends to be measurably more confident on data it has seen before than on similar data it hasn't. Their shadow models learned exactly that confidence gap, turning it into a working membership classifier.

This is a real, documented privacy risk, not an academic exercise. If a hospital trains a model on a cancer study or an HIV-status cohort, and an attacker can determine with confidence that a named person's record was in that training set, the model's own behavior has disclosed that person's participation — independent of whatever the model was actually built to predict. That is exactly the re-identification risk HIPAA and GDPR's special-category protections exist to prevent.

Extraction, inversion, and membership inference are all the same underlying fact wearing different clothes: a trained model is a lossy but exploitable compression of its training data, and anything it answers confidently is a potential leak channel. The next two lessons close that gap from two directions — limiting how much any one party can query a model, and bounding, mathematically, how much any single training record can influence it in the first place.
